documents.sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, describing the epidemic of 1519–1521, written before 1560
documents.text: In the course of the fifth year the pestilence began, O my children. First there was a cough, then the blood was corrupted, and the urine became yellow. The number of deaths at this time was truly terrible. The Chief Vakaki Ahmak died, and we ourselves were plunged in great darkness and great grief, our fathers and ancestors having contracted the plague, O my children. … Truly the number of deaths among the people was terrible, nor did the people escape from the pestilence. … The ancients and the fathers died alike, and the stench was such that men died of it alone. Then perished our fathers and ancestors. Half the people threw themselves into the ravines, and the dogs and foxes lived on the bodies of the men. The fear of death destroyed the old people, and the oldest son of the king died at the same time as his young brother. Thus did we become poor, O my children, and thus did we survive, being but a little child—and we were all that remained.
documents.translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885

documents.sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, entries for c. 1530–1548, written before 1560
documents.text: During this year frightful imposts were levied; they paid gold and silver before the face of Tunatiuh [Pedro de Alvarado], and there were demanded as tribute five hundred men and five hundred women to go to the gold washings; all the people were busy seeking gold. … All that, yes, all that, we ourselves witnessed, O my children. … The prince Don Jorge was appointed by the sole command of Tunatiuh. There was no council held nor assembly to confirm him. Tunatiuh gave his orders to the princes and they obeyed him; for, truly, he made himself feared. … In the course of the year the President Cerrado [Alonso López de Cerrato] arrived … When he arrived he condemned the Castilians; he set free the slaves and prisoners of the Castilians, diminished by one-half the imposts, put an end to forced labor, and obliged the Castilians to pay all for their work, little or great. This Prince Cerrado truly solaced the afflictions of our nation; for I, myself, O my children, was a witness of the many miseries which we endured.
documents.translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885

documents.sourceLine: The Annals of the Cakchiquels, history of the Kaqchikel Maya kingdom of Guatemala kept by the Xahila family of Kaqchikel nobles; this part written by a family member who lived through the events, entries for 1556–1557, written before 1560
documents.text: There were then three rulers, the Prince Ramirez, the Doctor Mercia and Louaisa. They held court at Panchoy. In the 14th month of the year, after this day of Sanctiago, there came an order from Ramirez. He imposed a tribute on members of the nobility among the people. He also made provision for the surplusage of the tribute. There had never been a surplus under the chiefs; it was known to be stolen, but no one knew by whom. The maize tax was reduced and that of roast fowls, and none of the chiefs could steal anything from the surplus. … Twenty days after the promulgation of the order of Ramirez, the Book of the Doctrina was published, on the day of Saints, a Monday; but many would not accept the Doctrina, but refused it. … Don Juan Juarez and Francisco Pez Martin were chosen as Alcaldes, to issue orders. (Note by a later writer: These were the first Alcaldes, and with them began the elections.)
documents.translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels, 1885

documents.sourceLine: Maya chronicle of the katuns (twenty-year periods) from the Book of Chilam Balam of Tizimin, a community record kept in Yucatec Maya by unnamed Maya scribes, late sixteenth century
documents.text: The fourth ahau; the pestilence, the general death, took place in the fortress. The second ahau; the smallpox took place. … 14. The eleventh ahau; foreigners arrived—mighty men from the east; they came, they arrived here in this land. The ninth ahau; Christianity began; baptism took place; also in this katun came the first bishop Toral; the year which was passing was—1544. 15. The seventh ahau; bishop Landa died in this katun. 16. The fifth ahau; the Fathers settled at Mani; the year that was passing was 1550; in the year 1552 they settled upon the water. 17. 1559; this year came the auditor and built the Hospital. 18. 1560; this year arrived Doctor Quixada, the first governor here in this land. 19. 1562; this year took place the hanging. 20. 1563; this year came Mariscal. 21. 1569; this year smallpox occurred.
documents.translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Maya Chronicles, 1882

documents.sourceLine: Nakuk Pech (baptized Don Pablo Pech), Maya noble and hereditary chief of Chac Xulub Chen in Yucatán, history of his town and of the conquest, c. 1562
documents.text: …I, Nakuk Pech, was taken and given to Don Julian Doncel the Encomendero, the first lord of the town Chac Xulub Chen, the first Encomendero, and my hand was given him by the captain Don Francisco de Montejo, and I was given for a chief to Don Julian Doncel, in his hand, and I began to take tribute for the holy fathers. … when I entered the water and received baptism, I was called Don Pablo Pech; and I ceased to be called Nakuk Pech; [we first] chiefs were created hidalgos by the captains when possession was first taken of this province, and we first paid tribute to the foreigners, and possession was given to us by God and the ruling king; and our descendants are hidalgos, and all our sons, until the time shall come when the world shall end … and I was also the first to receive the rod of the justicia, because I went to aid the Word of God and our great Lord the ruling king
documents.translation: Translated by Daniel G. Brinton, The Maya Chronicles, 1882

documents.sourceLine: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Spanish soldier in Cortés's army, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, written c. 1568 about 1519–1521
documents.text: But to return to Narvaez. He happened to have a negro servant with him ill with the smallpox, through whom this terrific disease, which, according to the accounts of the inhabitants, was previously unknown in the country, spread itself through New Spain, where it created the greater devastation, from the poor Indians, in their ignorance, solely applying cold water as a remedy, with which they constantly bathed themselves; so that vast numbers were cut off before they had the blessing of being received into the bosom of the Christian church. … About this time thousands of people were carried off by the smallpox, and among them numbers of caziques; and Cortes, as though he had been lord of the whole country, appointed the new caziques, but made a point of nominating those who had the best claim.
documents.translation: Translated by John Ingram Lockhart, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, 1844

documents.sourceLine: Thomas Hariot, English scientist with the Roanoke colony of 1585–1586, A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia, 1588 (adapted)
documents.text: There was no town where we had any subtle device practised against us, we leaving it unpunished or not revenged … but that within a few days after our departure from every such town, the people began to die very fast, and many in short space; in some towns about twenty, in some forty, in some sixty, and in one six score, which in truth was very many in respect of their numbers. … The disease also so strange, that they neither knew what it was, nor how to cure it; the like by the report of the oldest men in the country never happened before, time out of mind. … Insomuch that when some of the inhabitants which were our friends and especially the Wiroans [chief] Wingina had observed such effects in four or five towns to follow their wicked practices, they were persuaded that it was the work of our God through our means, and that we by him might kill and slay whom we would without weapons and not come near them.
documents.original: There was no towne where we had any subtile deuise practised against vs, we leauing it vnpunished or not reuenged … but that within a few dayes after our departure from euerie such towne, the people began to die very fast, and many in short space; in some townes about twentie, in some fourtie, in some sixtie, & in one sixe score, which in trueth was very manie in respect of their numbers. … The disease also so strange, that they neither knew what it was, nor how to cure it; the like by the report of the oldest men in the countrey neuer happened before, time out of minde. … Insomuch that when some of the inhabitantes which were our friends & especially the Wiroans Wingina had obserued such effects in foure or fiue towns to follow their wicked practises, they were preswaded that it was the worke of our God through our meanes, and that wee by him might kil and slai whom we would without weapons and not come neere them.

documents.sourceLine: William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony, Of Plymouth Plantation, entry for 1634 on the Native people near the colony's trading house on the Connecticut River, written c. 1640s (adapted)
documents.text: This spring, also, those Indians that lived about their trading house there fell sick of the small pox, and died most miserably; for a sorer disease cannot befall them; they fear it more than the plague; for usually they that have this disease have them in abundance, and for want of bedding and linen and other helps, they fall into a lamentable condition, as they lie on their hard mats, the pox breaking and mattering, and running one into another, their skin cleaving (by reason thereof) to the mats they lie on … and then being very sore, what with cold and other distempers, they die like rotten sheep. … The chief Sachem himself now died, and almost all his friends and kindred. But by the marvellous goodness and providence of God not one of the English was so much as sick, or in the least measure tainted with this disease, though they daily did these offices for them for many weeks together.
documents.original: This spring, also, those Indeans that lived aboute their trading house there fell sick of ye small poxe, and dyed most miserably; for a sorer disease cannot befall them; they fear it more then ye plague; for usualy they that have this disease have them in abundance, and for wante of bedding & lin̅ing and other helps, they fall into a lamentable condition, as they lye on their hard matts, ye poxe breaking and mattering, and runing one into another, their skin cleaving (by reason therof) to the matts they lye on … and then being very sore, what with could and other distempers, they dye like rotten sheep. … The cheefe Sachem him selfe now dyed, & allmost all his freinds & kinred. But by ye marvelous goodnes & providens of God not one of ye English was so much as sicke, or in ye least measure tainted with this disease, though they dayly did these offices for them for many weeks togeather.

documents.sourceLine: John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, journal entries for November 1633 to January 1634
documents.text: A great mortality among the Indians. Chickatabot, the sagamore of Naponsett, died, and many of his people. The disease was the small pox. … John Sagamore died of the small pox, and almost all his people; (above thirty buried by Mr. Maverick … of Winesemett in one day). The towns in the bay took away many of the children; but most of them died soon after. … Divers of them, in their sickness, confessed that the Englishmen's God was a good God; and that, if they recovered, they would serve him. … They informed us, that the small pox was gone as far as any Indian plantation was known to the west, and much people dead of it, by reason whereof they could have no trade. At Naragansett, by the Indians' report, there died seven hundred; but, beyond Pascataquack, none to the eastward.

documents.sourceLine: Bartolomé de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomienda holder who campaigned for Indigenous rights, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written 1542, published 1552
documents.text: The Spaniards first assaulted the innocent Sheep, so qualified by the Almighty, as is premention'd, like most cruel Tygers, Wolves and Lions hunger-starv'd, studying nothing, for the space of Forty Years, after their first landing, but the Massacre of these Wretches … that of Three Millions of Persons, which lived in Hispaniola itself, there is at present but the inconsiderable remnant of scarce Three Hundred. Nay the Isle of Cuba, which extends as far, as Valledolid in Spain is distant from Rome, lies now uncultivated, like a Desert, and intomb'd in its own Ruins. … whereas, when the Spaniards first arriv'd here, about Five Hundred Thousand Men dwelt in it, they are now cut off, some by slaughter, and others ravished away by Force and Violence, to work in the Mines of Hispanioloa [Hispaniola], which was destitute of Native Inhabitants
documents.translation: Translated in Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours (London, 1689), translator not named

documents.sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca", son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, raised in Cuzco and writing in Spain, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609
documents.text: Many cows were introduced soon after the conquest, and spread over the whole country. The same must have been the case with pigs and sheep; for I remember having seen them at Cuzco, when I was quite a child. … The first bullocks I saw at the plough were in the valley of Cuzco in the year 1550, one year more or less … A whole army of Indians took me to see them, who came from all parts, astonished at a sight so wonderful and novel for them and for me. They said that the Spaniards were too idle to work, and that they forced those great animals to do their work for them. … When they began to sell cows, the prices were from two hundred pesos, lowering gradually as the beasts became more plentiful, until the price fell suddenly to what they now sell at. … In 1559 I saw cows bought at Cuzco for seventeen pesos or twenty and a half ducats, rather less than more.
documents.translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 2, 1871

documents.sourceLine: José de Acosta, Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru and Mexico 1572–1587, The Natural and Moral History of the Indies, 1590 (adapted)
documents.text: I find there are three kinds of beasts at the Indies, whereof some have been carried from Spain; others are of the same kind we have in Europe, and yet not carried by the Spaniards; and others are proper to the Indies, whereof there are none in Spain. Of the first kind are sheep, kine [cattle], goats, swine, horses, asses, dogs, cats, and other such beasts, for there are of all these kinds at the Indies. … These wild kine have so multiplied in Santo Domingo and thereabouts, that they troop together in the fields and woods by thousands, having no master to whom they appertain. They hunt these beasts only for their hides … In the fleet, the year 1587, there came from Santo Domingo 35444 hides, and from New Spain 64350, which they value at 96532 pieces, so as when they discharge one of these fleets it is admirable to behold the river of Seville, and in the arsenal (where they unlade) so many hides …
documents.original: I finde there are three kindes of beasts at the Indies, whereof some have been carried from Spaine ; others are of the same kinde we have in Europe, and yet not carried by the Spaniardes ; and others are proper to the Indies, whereof there are none in Spaine. Of the first kinde are sheepe, kine, goates, swine, horses, asses, dogs, cattes, and other such beasts, for there are of all these kindes at the Indies. … These wilde kine have so multiplied in Santo Domingo and thereabouts, that they troope together in the fields and woods by thousands, having no master to whom they appertaine. They hunt these beasts onely for their hides … In the fleet, the yere 1587, there came from Santo Domingo 35444 hides, and from New Spaine 64350, which they value at 96532 peeces, so as when they discharge one of these fleetes it is admirable to behold the river of Seville, and in the arsenall (where they vnlade) so many hides …
documents.translation: Translated by Edward Grimston, 1604; edited by Clements R. Markham, The Natural & Moral History of the Indies, vol. 1, Hakluyt Society, 1880

documents.sourceLine: Peter Martyr d'Anghiera, Italian humanist at the Spanish court who questioned returning explorers and colonists, De Orbe Novo, First Decade, c. 1510
documents.text: The bread made by the natives is found, by those who are accustomed to our wheat bread, to be insufficiently nourishing and therefore they lose their strength. The King consequently issued a recent decree, ordering that wheat should be sown in different places and at different seasons. The harvest produced nothing but straw, similar to twigs, and with little grain; although what there is, is large and well formed. This also applies to the pastures where the grass grows as high as the crops; thus the cattle become extraordinarily fat, but their flesh loses its flavour; their muscles become flabby, and they are, so to say, watery. With pigs it is just the contrary; for they are healthy and of an agreeable flavour. This is due doubtless to certain of the island's fruits they greedily devour. Pork is about the only kind of meat bought in the markets. The pigs have rapidly increased, but they have become wild since they are no longer kept by swineherds.
documents.translation: Translated by Francis Augustus MacNutt, De Orbe Novo: The Eight Decades of Peter Martyr d'Anghera, 1912

documents.sourceLine: Filippo Pigafetta, Italian writer, setting down the account of Duarte Lopes, a Portuguese merchant who lived in the Kingdom of Kongo 1578–1583, A Report of the Kingdom of Congo, 1591 (adapted)
documents.text: The whole plain is fruitful and cultivated, having verdant meadows and large trees, and produces grain of various kinds. The best grain is called Luco, which is like mustard seed, but larger. This is ground in a handmill, and from the white flour excellent bread is made, and such as is not even inferior to corn [wheat], although only the latter is used in the celebration of mass. … Here is also the best white grain, called mazza di Congo, that is, grain of Congo, and maize, which is of so little value that they give it to pigs, rice being likewise little thought of. Maize is known as mazza Manputo, that is, Portugal grain.
documents.original: The whole plain is fruitful and cultivated, having verdant meadows and large trees, and produces grain of various kinds. The beft grain is called Luco, which is like muftard feed, but larger. This is ground in a handmill, and from the white flour excellent bread is made, and fuch as is not even inferior to corn, although only the latter is ufed in the celebration of mafs. … Here is alfo the beft white grain, called mazza di Congo, that is, grain of Congo, and maize, which is of fo little value that they give it to pigs, rice being likewife little thought of. Maize is known as mazza Manputo, that is, Portugal grain.
documents.translation: Translated by Margarite Hutchinson, A Report of the Kingdom of Congo, 1881

documents.sourceLine: John Gerard, English herbalist and gardener, The Herball or Generall Historie of Plantes (first published 1597), chapter "Of Turkie Corne" as revised by the London apothecary Thomas Johnson for the 1636 edition
documents.text: [T]hese kinds of grain were first brought into Spaine, and then into other provinces of Europe: not (as some suppose) out of Asia minor, which is the Turks dominions; but out of America and the Islands adjoining, as out of Florida, and Virginia or Norembega, where they use to sow or set it to make bread of it, where it growes much higher than in other countries. It is planted in the gardens of these Northern regions, where it commeth to ripenesse when the summer falleth out to be faire and hot; as my selfe have seen by proof in myne owne garden. … Turky wheat doth nourish far lesse than either wheat, rie, barly, or otes. The bread which is made thereof is meanely white, without bran: it is hard and dry as Bisket is, and hath in it no clamminesse at all … whereas we may easily judge, that it nourisheth but little, and is of hard and evill digestion, a more convenient food for swine than for man.

documents.sourceLine: James I, king of England and Scotland, A Counterblaste to Tobacco, 1604 (adapted)
documents.text: And now good countrymen let us (I pray you) consider, what honour or policy can move us to imitate the barbarous and beastly manners of the wild, godless, and slavish Indians, especially in so vile and stinking a custom? … Now how you are by this custom disabled in your goods, let the gentry of this land bear witness, some of them bestowing three, some four hundred pounds a year upon this precious stink, which I am sure might be bestowed upon many far better uses. … The public use whereof, at all times, and in all places, hath now so far prevailed, as divers men very sound both in judgement, and complexion, have been at last forced to take it also without desire … A custom loathsome to the eye, hateful to the Nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the Lungs, and in the black stinking fume thereof, nearest resembling the horrible Stygian smoke of the pit that is bottomless.
documents.original: And now good Countrey men let vs (I pray you) consider, what honour or policie can mooue vs to imitate the barbarous and beastly maners of the wilde, godlesse, and slauish Indians, especially in so vile and stinking a custome? … Now how you are by this custome disabled in your goods, let the gentry of this land beare witnesse, some of them bestowing three, some foure hundred pounds a yeere[J] vpon this precious stinke, which I am sure might be bestowed vpon many farre better vses. … The publike vse whereof, at all times, and in all places, hath now so farre preuailed, as diuers men very sound both in iudgement, and complexion, haue bene at last forced to take it also without desire … A custome lothsome to the eye, hatefull to the Nose, harmefull to the braine, dangerous to the Lungs, and in the blacke stinking fume thereof, neerest resembling the horrible Stigian smoke of the pit that is bottomelesse.

documents.sourceLine: Henry Hawks, English merchant who lived five years in New Spain, report on New Spain written for Richard Hakluyt, 1572 (adapted)
documents.text: There is in New Spain a marvellous increase of cattle, which daily do increase, and they are of a greater growth than ours are. You may have a great steer that hath an hundred weight of tallow in his belly for sixteen shillings; and some one man hath 2000 head of cattle of his own. They sell the hides unto the merchants, who lade into Spain as many as may be well spared. … They have many horses, and mares, and mules, which the Spaniards brought thither. … This Maize is the greatest maintenance which the Indian hath, and also all the common people of the Spaniards. And their horses and mules which labour, cannot be without the same. … If the Miners should be without it, they could not labour their mines: for all their servants eat none other bread, but only of this Maize, and it is made in cakes, as they make oaten cakes, in some places of England.
documents.original: There is in New Spaine a maruellous increase of cattle, which daily do increase, and they are of a greater growth then ours are. You may haue a great steere that hath an hundred weight of tallow in his belly for sixteene shillings; and some one man hath 2000 head of cattel of his owne. They sell the hides vnto the merchants, who lade into Spaine as many as may be well spared. … They haue many horses, and mares, and mules, which the Spaniards brought thither. … This Maiz is the greatest maintenance which the Indian hath, and also all the common people of the Spaniards. And their horses and mules which labour, cannot be without the same. … If the Miners should bee without it, they coulde not labour their mines: for all their seruants eate none other bread, but onely of this Maize, and it is made in cakes, as they make oaten cakes, in some places of England.

documents.sourceLine: Richard Ligon, English royalist exile who helped manage a sugar plantation on Barbados 1647–1650, A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbados, 1657
documents.text: …which had in it 500 Acres of Land, with a faire dwelling house, an Ingenio [sugar mill] plac’t in a roome of 400 foot square; a boyling house, filling roome, Cisterns, and Still-house … Houses for Negroes and Indian slaves, with 96 Negroes, and three Indian women, with their Children; 28 Christians, 45 Cattle for worke, 8 Milch Cowes, a dosen Horses and Mares, 16 Assinigoes [donkeys]. … In this plantation of 500 acres of land, there was imployed for sugar somewhat more then 200 acres; above 80 acres for pasture, 120 for wood, 30 for Tobacco, 5 for Ginger, as many for Cotton wool, and 70 acres for provisions; viz. Corne, Potatoes, Plantines, Cassavie, and Bonavist … The Iland is divided into three sorts of men, viz. Masters, Servants, and slaves. The slaves and their posterity, being subject to their Masters for ever, are kept and preserv’d with greater care then the servants, who are theirs but for five yeers, according to the law of the Iland.

documents.sourceLine: Pero de Magalhães de Gândavo, Portuguese official who lived in Brazil, History of the Province of Santa Cruz (Brazil), 1576
documents.text: …there are many others who are scattered about on the sugar mills and ranches, here as in the other Captaincies, all the surrounding territory being settled. … for the inhabitants are much favoured and aided by the Indians of the land from among whom they get an infinite number of slaves with whom they work their farms. … The first thing they try to obtain is slaves to work the farms; and any one who succeeds in obtaining two pairs or a half-dozen of them (although he may not have another earthly possession) has the means to sustain his family in a respectable way; for one fishes for him, another hunts for him, and the rest cultivate and till his fields, and consequently there is no expense for the maintenance of his slaves or of his household. … one may infer how very extensive are the estates of those who own two hundred or three hundred slaves, for there are many colonists who have that number or more.
documents.translation: Translated by John B. Stetson Jr., The Histories of Brazil, Cortes Society, 1922

documents.sourceLine: Miles Philips, English sailor on John Hawkins's slaving voyage of 1567–1568, later a prisoner in New Spain, account written after his return in 1582 (adapted)
documents.text: And being ready to depart from the Sea coast, there was a Negro sent as an Ambassador to our General, from a King of the Negroes, which was oppressed with other Kings his bordering neighbours, desiring our General to grant him succour and aid against those his enemies, which … our General granted unto, and went himself in person a land … and the said King which had requested our aid, did join his force with ours, so that thereby our General assaulted, and set fire upon a Town of the said King his enemies, in which there was at the least the number of eight or ten thousand Negroes … there were taken prisoners to the number of eight or nine hundred, which our General ought to have had for his share … but our General notwithstanding finding himself to have now very near the number of 500. Negroes thought it best without longer abode to depart with them, and such merchandise as he had from the coast of Africa, towards the West Indies
documents.original: And being ready to depart from the Sea coast, there was a Negro sent as an Ambassadour to our Generall, from a King of the Negros, which was oppressed with other Kings his bordering neighbours, desiring our Generall to grant him succour and ayde against those his enemies, which … our Generall granted vnto, and went himselfe in person a lande … and the said King which had requested our ayde, did ioyne his force with ours, so that thereby our Generall assaulted, and set fire vpon a Towne of the said King his enemies, in which there was at the least the number of eight or ten thousand Negros … there were taken prisoners to the number of eight or nine hundreth, which our Generall ought to haue had for his share … but our Generall notwithstanding finding himselfe to haue nowe very neere the number of 500. Negros thought it best without longer abode to depart with them, and such marchandize as hee had from the coast of Africa, towards the West Indies

documents.sourceLine: Henry Hawks, English merchant who lived five years in New Spain, report on New Spain written for Richard Hakluyt, 1572 (adapted)
documents.text: The Indians have the friars in great reverence: the occasion is, that by them and by their means they are free and out of bondage; which was so ordained by Charles the emperor: which is the occasion that now there is not so much gold and silver coming into Europe as there was while the Indians were slaves. For when they were in bondage they could not choose but do their task every day, and bring their master so much metal out of their mines: but now they must be well paid, and much entreated to have them work. So it hath been, and is a great hindrance to the owners of the mines, and to the king's quinto or custom. … A good owner of mines must have at the least an hundred slaves to carry and to stamp his metals … And the mines fall daily in decay, and of less value: and the occasion is, the few Indians that men have to labour their mines.
documents.original: The Indians haue the friers in great reuerence: the occasion is, that by them and by there meanes they are free and out of bondage; which was so ordeined by Charles the emperor: which is the occasion that now there is not so much gold and siluer comming into Europe as there was while the Indians were slaues. For when they were in bondage they could not chuse but doe their taske euery day, and bring their master so much metall out of their mines: but now they must be well payed, and much intreated to haue them worke. So it hath bene, and is a great hinderance to the owners of the mines, and to the kings quinto or custome. … A good owner of mines must haue at the least an hundred slaues to cary and to stampe his metals … And the mines fall dayly in decay, and of lesse value: and the occasion is, the few Indians that men haue to labour their mines.

documents.sourceLine: Bartolomé de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomienda holder who campaigned for Indigenous rights, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, on Hispaniola, written 1542, published 1552
documents.text: The Warlike Engagements being over, and the Inhabitants all swept away, they divided among themselves the Young Men, Women, and Children reserved promiscuously for that purpose, one obtained thirty, another forty, to this Man one hundred were disposed, to the other two hundred, and the more one was in favor with the domineering Tyrant (which they styled Governor) the more he became Master of, upon this pretence, and with this Proviso, that he should see them instructed in the Catholick Religion … they sent the Males to the Mines to dig and bring away the Gold, which is an intollerable labor; but the Women they made use of to Manure and Till the ground … The Men died in Mines, hunger starved and oppressed with labor, and the Women perished in the Fields, harrassed and broken with the like Evils and Calamities: Thus an infinite number of Inhabitants that formerly peopled this Island were exterminated and dwindled away to nothing by such Consumptions.
documents.translation: Translated in Popery Truly Display'd in its Bloody Colours (London, 1689), translator not named

documents.sourceLine: Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca", son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, raised in Cuzco and writing in Spain, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609
documents.text: One of the chief things that have happened in the Indies, which must not be forgotten, is the introduction of Negroes, whom the Spaniards have brought there as slaves to work for them; for there were none in my country before the conquest. … The sons of a Spaniard by an Indian woman, or of an Indian by a Spanish woman are called Mestizos, which means that we are a mixture of both nations. It was adopted by the first Spaniards who had children by Indian women; and, being a name given by our parents, I call myself by it with open mouth, and pride myself upon it. But the Indians look upon it as an insult, if anyone calls them Mestizos. … All these names, and others which I do not mention to avoid being tedious, have been invented in my country to designate the generations that have risen up since the arrival of the Spaniards; and we may say that the Spaniards brought them with the other things, as they were not there before.
documents.translation: Translated by Clements R. Markham, First Part of the Royal Commentaries of the Yncas, vol. 2, 1871

documents.sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, 1648
documents.text: In all the Dominions of the King of Spain in America, there are two sorts of Spaniards more opposite one to another then in Europe the Spaniard is opposite to the French, or to the Hollander, or to the Portingall; To wit, they that are born in any parts of Spain and goe thither, and they that are borne there of Spanish parents, whom the Spaniards, to distinguish them from themselves, terme Criolio's, signifying the Natives of that Countrey. … The cause of this deadly hatred hath proceeded from a jealousie which the Spaniards have ever had of the Criolio's, that they would faine withdraw themselves first from the commerce with Spain, and secondly, from the Government which is laid upon them; which is such, that the Criolio's must be alwaies under, and a subject, alwaies governed, but scarce any a Governour. Never yet was there seen any Criolio made Viceroy of Mexico, or Peru … And not onely thus are they kept from offices, but daily affronted by the Spaniards as uncapable of any Government, and termed halfe Indians by them.

documents.sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on the city of Cuzco
documents.text: The city has a large population, with over 3,000 Spaniards, many knights and nobles, encomenderos, descendants of the earliest pioneers in that Kingdom, together with many other Spaniards of honorable, distinguished, and middle class, and mestizos, sons of Spaniards and Indian women … from among whom have arisen very valiant and courageous warriors, servants of His Majesty who suffer great trials at all crises—all these form a … very illustrious republic. In this imperial city there is a large Indian population, nobility and commoners, comprising over 14,000 residents, not counting many others who come in from the adjoining provinces to render service in the city, plus large numbers of Negro slaves and mulattoes whom the city residents keep for their service in the city and on their farms, for they have cattle ranches, sugar mills, vineyards, and fields of wheat, corn, and other cereals and crops, and troops of mules for traffic to Lima and other points.
documents.translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942

documents.sourceLine: Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa, Spanish naval officers sent by the king to South America 1735–1744, A Voyage to South America, on the inhabitants of Quito, 1748
documents.text: This city is very populous, and has, among its inhabitants, some families of high rank and distinction; though their number is but small considering its extent, the poorer class bearing here too great a proportion. The former are the descendants either of the original conquerors, or of presidents, auditors, or other persons of character, who at different times came over from Spain invested with some lucrative post … The commonalty may be divided into four classes; Spaniards or Whites, Mestizos, Indians or Natives, and Negroes, with their progeny. … The name of Spaniard here has a different meaning from that of Chapitone or European, as properly signifying a person descended from a Spaniard without a mixture of blood. Many Mestizos, from the advantage of a fresh complexion, appear to be Spaniards more than those who are so in reality; and from only this fortuitous advantage are accounted as such. … at Quito the degrees of Mestizos are not carried so far back; for, even in the second or third generations, when they acquire the European colour, they are considered as Spaniards.
documents.translation: Translated by John Adams, A Voyage to South America, 1758 (fourth edition, 1806)

documents.sourceLine: Miles Philips, English sailor left in New Spain in 1568 and handed out as a servant to Spanish gentlemen, account written after his return in 1582 (adapted)
documents.text: The gentlemen that thus took us for their servants or slaves, did new apparel us throughout, with whom we abode, doing such service as they appointed us unto, which was for the most part to attend upon them at the table … for in that country no Spaniard will serve one another, but they are all of them attended and served by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaves during their life. … Afterwards many of us were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to do, and to be as overseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of us did profit and gain greatly … Sundry weeks we did gain so much by this means besides our wages, that many of us became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or four thousand Pesos
documents.original: The gentlemen that thus tooke vs for their seruants or slaues, did new apparell vs through out, with whom we abode, doing such service as they appointed vs vnto, which was for the most part to attend vpon them at the table … for in that countrey no Spaniard will serue one another, but they are all of them attended and serued by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaues during their life. … Afterwards many of vs were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to doe, and to be as ouerseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of vs did profite and gaine greatly … Sundry weeks we did gaine so much by this means besides our wages, that many of vs became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or foure thousand Pezos

documents.sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, on Mexico City, 1648
documents.text: Both men and women are excessive in their apparell, using more silkes then stuffes and cloth; pretious Stones and Pearles further much this their vaine ostentation; a hat-band and rose made of Diamonds in a Gentlemans hat is common, and a hat-band of Pearles is ordinary in a Tradesman; nay a Blackmore or Tauny young maide and slave will make hard shift but shee will bee in fashion with her Neckchaine and Bracelets of Pearls, and her Eare-bobs of some considerable Jewels. The attire of this baser sort of people of Blackmores and Mulatta's (which are of a mixt nature, of Spaniards and Blackmores) is so light, and their carriage so enticing, that many Spaniards even of the better sort (who are too too prone to Venery) disdaine their Wives for them.

documents.sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on Cartagena and Lima
documents.text: The city contains more than 1,500 Spanish residents, not counting mestizos, mulattoes, free Negroes and other categories, and the population is increasing … There is another company of free creole colored men, with a Captain appointed by His Majesty and 600 soldiers, as good as Spaniards and in their very image. These are employed in the handling of the artillery and other matters in His Majesty’s service, like trench and fascine work. … [In Lima] there are 32 municipal companies, not counting 22 appointed by the Viceroy to enroll men … and there are 3 of mulattoes and 2 of free Negroes, persons who are necessary and important for the work
documents.translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942

documents.sourceLine: Catalina de Erauso, Basque woman who fled a convent and lived as a man, serving as a soldier in Peru and Chile, memoir attributed to her, c. 1626
documents.text: The lady was a half-breed, the daughter of a Spaniard and an Indian woman. She was a widow, a good-natured soul, who seeing me and hearing of my calamity and misery, took pity on me and received me kindly. … and had vast herds and flocks; and as, apparently, few Spaniards ever pass that way, it seems that she cast her eye on me for her daughter. … A few days later she gave me to understand that she would be willing for me to marry a daughter of hers who lived there with her, and who was very black … I vowed myself enchanted at a condescension so undeserved, and fell at her feet, declaring that she might command me as a creature of hers snatched from destruction. I continued to serve her to the best of my powers. She dressed me out like a beau, and confidingly entrusted me with her house and belongings.
documents.translation: Translated by James Fitzmaurice-Kelly, The Nun Ensign, 1908

documents.sourceLine: Philip II, king of Spain, royal decree (cédula) to the viceroy and Audiencia of New Spain about Diego Díaz del Castillo, son of the conquistador Bernal Díaz, Madrid, 1565
documents.text: Diego Diaz del Castillo has presented me an account of how Bernal Diaz del Castillo, his father, was one of the first explorers and conquerors of that City of Mexico and of New Spain … In consideration of these, and of the fact that he was the son of such a conqueror, poor, and in need, our former viceroy of that land, Don Luis de Velasco, commanded that he be given in our name a gratuity of one hundred and fifty dollars in common gold … it is our determined will that you appoint and prefer him, as a son of a conqueror, to one of the corregimientos and positions made mention of above in the said provinces of Tlascala, Tepeaca, Chalco, Cholula, Jilotepeque, or to any other position which may be very good, honorable, and profitable. … for by appointing him to offices and other positions in our service he may serve us and be honored and benefited. And in other appointments in that land you will bear this order in mind and appoint like persons to them.
documents.translation: Translated in Charles W. Hackett, ed., Historical Documents Relating to New Mexico, Nueva Vizcaya, and Approaches Thereto, vol. 1, 1923

documents.sourceLine: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and king of Spain, the New Laws for the government of the Indies and the good treatment of the Indians, 1542
documents.text: Item, We ordain and command that from henceforward for no cause of war nor any other whatsoever, though it be under title of rebellion, nor by ransom nor in other manner can an Indian be made a slave, and we will that they be treated as our vassals of the Crown of Castile since such they are. No person can make use of the Indians by way of Naboria or Tapia or in any other manner against their will. … Because report has been made to us that owing to the pearl fisheries not having been conducted in a proper manner deaths of many Indians and Negroes have ensued, We command that no free Indian be taken to the said fishery under pain of death … Moreover, We ordain and command that from henceforward no Viceroy, Governor, Audiencia, discoverer, or any other person have power to allot Indians in encomienda by new provision … neither by vacancy nor inheritance, but that the person dying who held the said Indians, they revert to our Royal Crown.
documents.translation: Translated in Henry Stevens, ed., The New Laws of the Indies, 1893

documents.sourceLine: Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa, Spanish Carmelite friar who spent much of his life in Spanish America and travelled from Mexico to Peru in 1612–1622, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, written 1628–1629, on the mita (forced labour draft) for the silver mines of Potosí
documents.text: These Indians are sent out every year under a captain whom they choose in each village or tribe, for him to take them and oversee them for the year each has to serve; every year they have a new election, for as some go out, others come in. This works out very badly, with great losses and gaps in the quotas of Indians, the villages being depopulated; and this gives rise to great extortions and abuses on the part of the inspectors toward the poor Indians, ruining them and thus depriving the caciques and chief Indians of their property and carrying them off in chains because they do not fill out the mita assignment, which they cannot do … These mita Indians earn each day, or there is paid each one for his labor, 4 reals. Besides these there are others not under obligation, who are mingados or hire themselves out voluntarily: these each get from 12 to 16 reals, and some up to 24, according to their reputation of wielding the pick and knowing how to get the ore out.
documents.translation: Translated by Charles Upson Clark, Compendium and Description of the West Indies, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections vol. 102, 1942

documents.sourceLine: Thomas Gage, English Dominican friar who lived in Mexico and Guatemala 1625–1637 and later turned Protestant and wrote for an English readership hostile to Spain, The English-American, or A New Survey of the West-Indias, on Guatemala, 1648
documents.text: The Spaniards that live about that Country … alleadge that all their trading, and farming, is for the good of the Common-wealth, and therefore whereas there are not Spaniards enough for so ample and large a Countrey to doe all their work, and all are not able to buy slaves and Blackmores, they stand in need of the Indians help to serve them for their pay and hire; whereupon it hath been considered, that a partition of Indian labourers be made every Monday, or Sonday in the afternoon to the Spaniards … If complaint be made by any Spaniard that such and such an Indian did run away from him … the Indian must be brought, and surely tied to a post by his hands in the Market place, and there be whipped upon his bare backe. But if the poor Indian complaine that the Spaniards cousened and cheated him of his shovell, axe, bill, mantle, or wages, no justice shall be executed against the cheating Spaniard … Thus are the poore Indians sold for three pence a peece for a whole weeks slavery

documents.sourceLine: Pero de Magalhães de Gândavo, Portuguese official who lived in Brazil, History of the Province of Santa Cruz (Brazil), 1576
documents.text: Since these Indians covet certain things which come from the Kingdom of Portugal, namely, shirts, jerkins, iron tools, and similar things, they sell one another in exchange for these articles to the Portuguese; these, on the other hand, capture as many as they want and do them many injuries without any one's checking them [the Portuguese]. But now there is no longer this disorder in the land or the traffic in slaves as formerly. … the Fathers ordered and arranged with the Governours and Captains of the land that there should be no more trading in slaves in the same way as in the past … whatever slaves are newly come out of the sertao … all go first to the custom house where they examine them and ask them questions: who sold them and what were the terms of purchase; for no one has the right to sell them save their fathers … or those who have captured them in a just war; those whom they find acquired illegally, they set at liberty.
documents.translation: Translated by John B. Stetson Jr., The Histories of Brazil, Cortes Society, 1922

poolHints.why: A Kaqchikel Maya survivor describes the epidemic of 1519–1521 killing rulers and elders alike and leaving the community poor and leaderless.
A Kaqchikel noble records forced gold-washing labour under Alvarado, who named Maya rulers at will, and then a royal president freeing slaves and ending forced labour.
Kaqchikel nobles lose their exemption from tribute and their hold on its surplus, while Kaqchikel men are chosen for new Spanish-style offices as alcaldes in the first elections.
A Maya community record places smallpox and "the general death" before the arrival of the "mighty men from the east" and records smallpox again in 1569, alongside conversion and colonial rule.
A Maya chief keeps his rank by cooperating: he collects tribute for an encomendero, takes a Spanish name, and is made a hidalgo with the staff of local justice.
A conquistador traces smallpox to an African servant in Narváez's force and shows the epidemic killing Indigenous lords, which let Cortés choose their successors.
An English observer records Algonquian towns dying of an unknown disease after English visits, and Native leaders concluding that the English God was killing them.
A Puritan governor describes smallpox killing a Native community and its sachem while sparing the English, which he reads as God's providence.
The Massachusetts governor records smallpox killing Native leaders and whole villages across New England, ending the fur trade there and pushing survivors toward the English and their religion.
A Spanish friar blames the collapse of the Caribbean population on massacre and forced mining rather than disease, a counter-claim to the epidemic accounts.
A mestizo who grew up in Cuzco remembers the first plough oxen amazing Andean people and cattle multiplying until their price collapsed.
A Jesuit naturalist shows European livestock running wild in the Caribbean and tens of thousands of American cattle hides shipped to Seville each year.
Spanish settlers on Hispaniola struggle on Taíno bread, fail to grow wheat, and watch imported pigs multiply and go wild.
Maize from the Americas had reached Kongo by the 1580s under the name "Portugal grain", but people there still valued it so little they fed it to pigs.
An English herbal records maize grown in an English garden but judges it fit for pigs rather than people, showing how slowly Europeans accepted the crop.
The English king attacks tobacco, an American plant, as a habit copied from Native Americans that had spread through English society and drained the gentry's wealth.
An English merchant describes European cattle, horses and mules multiplying in Mexico while American maize remained the staple of Indians, poorer Spaniards and the mines.

A Barbados sugar estate combines enslaved Africans and Indians, European livestock, American food crops and cash crops, with slaves and their children bound to their masters for ever while servants served five years.
Portuguese settlers in Brazil build sugar mills and farms on enslaved Indigenous labour, which a royal official presents as the key to every colonist's prosperity.
Even a poor Portuguese settler could live "in a respectable way" once he owned a few slaves, so slave-owning was the route upward for colonists.
English slavers join a West African king's war to take hundreds of captives for sale in the Spanish Caribbean, linking African warfare to American labour demand.
A merchant reports that royal law freed Indigenous slaves so they now had to be paid, while mine owners still relied on slaves and suffered from a shrinking Indigenous workforce.
Population loss and the end of Indigenous slavery left mines short of workers, pushing owners toward enslaved labour.
Las Casas describes the first encomiendas: Taíno people parcelled out to Spaniards "to be instructed" and worked to death in mines and fields.
Forced labour in Hispaniola's gold mines and fields destroyed the Taíno population that Spaniards had first relied on.
A mestizo author explains that new names for people of mixed ancestry arose after the conquest, and that he is proud of "mestizo" while Indians take it as an insult.
Garcilaso counts the enslaved Africans brought "to work for them" and the mixed populations that followed among the chief changes the Spaniards brought to Peru.
Gage describes the bitter divide between Spaniards born in Spain and creoles born in America, who were kept out of the highest offices and insulted as "half Indians".
A friar ranks Cuzco's people from Spanish knights and encomenderos through mestizos to Indian nobles and commoners and enslaved Africans and mulattoes.
Cuzco's elite now ran cattle ranches, sugar mills, vineyards and wheat fields worked by enslaved Africans, showing Old World crops and animals rooted in the Andes.
Two Spanish officers describe Quito's ranked classes by ancestry and colour, and how light-skinned mestizos could pass as Spaniards within a few generations.
English prisoners given to Spaniards as servants were soon made overseers of Indian and African mine workers and grew rich, because in New Spain no European served another.
Mexico's mines ran on Indigenous labour drafted weekly and on enslaved Africans held for life, under European overseers.
In Mexico City enslaved and free women of African descent wore pearls and silks meant for their betters, using dress to claim a status the hierarchy denied them.
Free men of African descent in Cartagena and Lima served in their own militia companies, one under a captain appointed by the king, a recognised route to standing in colonial society.
A wealthy mestiza widow hopes to marry her dark-skinned daughter to a passing "Spaniard" (really Erauso, a woman living as a man), showing both marriage and disguise as ways around the hierarchy.
The American-born son of a conqueror has fallen into poverty, and the king orders that he and men like him be given offices, so creole status depended on royal favour.
The crown bans Indian slavery and forced service and orders encomiendas to return to the crown when holders die, an attempt to change the labour system from the top.
The law admits that forced labour in the pearl fisheries was killing Indians and Africans and protects only "free" Indians from it.
The Potosí mita emptied Andean villages and even ruined and chained Indigenous caciques who could not supply their quotas, while drafted workers earned a fraction of free wage labourers.

Gage shows the weekly repartimiento in Guatemala: Indian villages forced to hand over labourers to Spanish farmers who could not afford African slaves, with punishment for runaways and no justice for cheated workers.
In Portuguese Brazil, Indigenous people were enslaved through trade and raids until Jesuit pressure brought inspections that freed those taken illegally, though "just war" captives stayed slaves.

gaps: Toribio de Benavente (Motolinía), History of the Indians of New Spain (1541): no English translation published before 1930 or under an open licence was found (the Foster 1950 and Steck 1951 translations are in copyright). Not used.

Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex book 12 (the Nahua account of the 1520 smallpox epidemic): the English translations (Anderson and Dibble, 1955 onward; León-Portilla, The Broken Spears, 1962) are in copyright, and the Fordham page taken from The Broken Spears (mod/aztecs1.asp) does not include the smallpox passage. No Nahua account of the epidemic could be used; the Kaqchikel annals and the Maya chronicle of Tizimin are the Indigenous voices on disease instead.

Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, Natural History of the West Indies (1526): the full English translation (Stoudemire, 1959) is in copyright, and Richard Eden's partial 1555 translation was not checked for a usable transcription. Not used.

Pedro Cieza de León (Markham translations, 1864 and 1883): not used here, because his Potosí material belongs to cluster c's silver prompt. The Fordham page (mod/1540cieza.asp) covers only the Inca storehouse system.

Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa, Cartagena chapter (the named castes: Tercerones, Quarterones, Quinterones, "Salto atrás"): every archive.org scan checked (the 1758, 1806 and 1807 English editions) prints that chapter with the long s, and the OCR has errors in almost every line, so no excerpt could be matched cleanly. The document uses the Quito chapter of the 1806 fourth edition instead, which the OCR renders cleanly.
Richard Ligon (1657): the archive.org OCR of the 1657 print is unusable. The excerpt comes from the Project Gutenberg transcription (ebook 70489), which keeps the 1657 spelling.

Virginia slave laws of 1662 and 1705 (Hening's Statutes) and the French Code Noir (1685): not used. They concern English and French colonies, not the Spanish and Portuguese Americas named in the hierarchy prompt, and no openly licensed English translation of the Code Noir was found.

Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Reply to Sor Filotea (1691): no English translation published before 1930 or under an open licence was found (Wikisource has none; the Fordham link points only to an archived page of poems whose translation status is unknown). As a result, women's convent life is missing. The only woman author in this cluster is Catalina de Erauso.

Portuguese Brazil beyond Gândavo: no usable English text was found for António Vieira's sermons to enslaved sugar workers (1633) or for Antonil's Cultura e Opulência do Brasil (1711). Fernão Cardim (in Purchas, 1625) was not checked.

African voices: no African-authored text on American crops, the Columbian Exchange or plantation labour was found in a usable translation. Africa appears only through European observers (Duarte Lopes via Pigafetta, and Miles Philips on Hawkins's raid). Willem Bosman (1704; English 1705) reports that maize was brought to the Gold Coast by the Portuguese and that Africans there smoked Brazilian tobacco, but in all four archive.org scans checked, those passages have heavy long-s OCR errors. Bosman is left to cluster c, which lists him as a starting point.

Enslaved and free Africans in Spanish and Portuguese America speaking for themselves (for example Alonso de Sandoval's interviews, 1627): no usable translation was found. The race-caste and mobility groups rely on Spanish, English, mestizo and Maya observers.

Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui Salcamayhua, an Andean noble writing c. 1613 (Markham translation, 1873), describes the epidemic that killed Huayna Capac. He was born decades after it, so the account fails the rule that later accounts must come from people who lived through the events. Not used.
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala (1615) and Titu Cusi Yupanqui (1570): no English translation published before 1930 or under an open licence was found.

John Winthrop's 1634 letter ("the Lord hath cleared our title"): not found in volume 2 of the Life and Letters of John Winthrop (1864). His journal entries on the same smallpox epidemic are used instead (Hosmer edition, 1908).

John Gerard's Herball: the archive.org OCR of the 1597 black-letter edition is too noisy to match. The excerpt comes from Marcus Woodward's 1927 selection, which reprints the 1636 edition as revised by Thomas Johnson, so the document is dated 1636. The two editions differ in this chapter: in 1597 Gerard wrote that maize came "out of Asia which is in the Turkes Dominions, as also out of America", and Johnson corrected this to "not (as some suppose) out of Asia minor … but out of America".
